title: Why PPP projects fail and the need for sound process
objectives: Define project failure in PPP terms as a failure to achieve the expected Value for Money.
Classify failures by timing (before or after contract signature) and by severity (redefinition, cancellation, absolute or relative failure).
Identify the main threats to sound process management, including weak capacity and the absence of a PPP framework.
Match typical failure examples to the phase of the PPP process where their cause lies.
List the conditions that make a project acceptable and attractive to prospective bidders.

sections.heading: What counts as project failure
sections.body:
A PPP should only be procured when there is **strong evidence that it is the right project**. Like any project, it must be technically feasible, the best economic option for the public need, affordable, and commercially feasible (with real competition and bankable offers). On top of that, the PPP option should only be chosen when there is significant evidence that it will **add Value for Money (VfM)** compared with other procurement methods.

VfM can be lost in many ways: costs or benefits are estimated wrongly, the groundwork is poorly prepared, risks are not detected, the contract is badly structured or drafted, or the tender and the contract are badly managed. So the Guide gives a simple definition:

> **A failure to achieve the expected VfM is a project failure.**

Success means avoiding failure risks or reducing their effects. In essence, this is **effective risk management**. It requires three things:

1. **The project is the right project.** The best VfM option is selected and properly prioritised against other possible projects.
2. **PPP is the right delivery model.** The PPP route is likely to give better VfM than traditional procurement.
3. **The project is appraised, prepared, structured and managed well**, to limit bad effects on cost, time, scope and quality. Sometimes an independent appraiser is needed to keep the analysis objective.

VfM must be protected **throughout** planning, procurement and the whole life of the contract. This needs proper process management, suitable skills and resources, and standard approaches and good practice.

sections.heading: Types of failure: timing and severity
sections.body:
The Guide classifies failure by **when** it happens and **how serious** it is. There are two main stages: **before** the contract is signed at commercial close, and **after** it is signed. Note that reaching contract signature does **not** mean the PPP has succeeded; the contract can still fail during its life.

**Before contract signature** (during preparation, structuring or tender), there are two categories:

- the process is **suspended and the project is redefined**, fully (new scope, appraisal starts again) or partially (some scope or contract terms are refined);
- the process is **definitively cancelled**, at least as a PPP.

A decision part-way through **not** to go ahead as a PPP is **not a negative outcome**. That is exactly the purpose of progressive appraisal. But **the later the failure, the bigger the loss**. This is why the Guide recommends a step-by-step process with progressive approvals, a **gateway process**. The worst case before signature is **cancelling after the tender has been launched**: time and money are lost and the government's PPP reputation suffers.

**After contract signature**, there are two grades:

| Grade | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Absolute contract failure** | The government has to **rescue or re-tender** the contract, because the private partner is in **serious default** or the SPV goes **bankrupt** (the two can overlap). |
| **Relative project failure** | VfM is **partly lost**. The contract works, but not as well as expected. |

Relative failure can happen when performance is poor but the contract does not capture the lost value, when the private partner gets an unexpected benefit that should have been shared, or when an unforeseen event hits and the contract does not provide for it, or the government has not budgeted for the compensation due. A change of administration that withdraws political support can also reduce the perceived VfM.

sections.heading: Threats to sound process management
How a missing framework makes failure more likely
Examples of failure at each stage
What bidders need: the private sector view
sections.body:
A PPP needs private companies willing to sign a long-term contract and take significant risk, equity investors willing to invest, and banks willing to lend. Commercial feasibility, including **bankability**, is a necessary condition. But bidders care about **all** aspects of feasibility, not only their own return:

- if the project has **poor economic value** or weak government commitment, there is a higher chance of termination or renegotiation by a new government;
- bidders want the project to be **affordable**, because an unaffordable project increases the risk of **government breach**;
- they want a **reliable timetable** and a collaborative, well-managed process.

The Guide's Table 1.7 lists the conditions a project must meet to be acceptable and attractive to bidders:

| Condition | What bidders look for |
|---|---|
| Economically sound | The right solution; low use weakens public commitment and, in demand projects, revenue |
| Suitable as a PPP | Otherwise the risk structure is artificial, leading to no bids or later failure |
| Technically feasible | No technical risks that cannot be taken on |
| Commercially feasible | The payment ceiling or price covers costs, risk contingencies and a fair return |
| Bankable | Lenders and investors are willing to provide finance |
| Legally feasible | The structure clearly fits the legal framework, avoiding nullity or challenges |
| Affordable | Realistic approval of what the government can really pay |
| Properly prepared | Due diligence done; the government can meet its duties, e.g. right of way |
| Properly structured contract | Manageable risks, clear payment and performance regimes, protection from public breach |
| Properly structured tender | Balanced capacity requirements and transparent criteria that screen out unrealistic offers |

The message is that the government's interests and good bidders' interests largely **coincide**: both want a well-prepared, feasible, affordable project.

example.title: Illustrative case: the Northgate hospital PPP
example.body:
Imagine the health ministry of a fictional country announces a hospital PPP three months before an election. To meet the date, the team skips a proper appraisal and launches an open tender with a six-week bid period over the national holidays.

- Only one bid arrives. The land title for the site is then found to be disputed, and the tender is **cancelled after launch**. This is the most damaging failure before signature: time, money and reputation are lost.
- The team restarts with a **gateway process**. At the appraisal gateway the full CBA and affordability test show the scope is too large, so the project is **redefined** to a smaller hospital. This is a failure of the milder kind, and it is exactly what progressive appraisal is meant to catch.
- Years later, after signature, the contract works but its performance requirements cannot be measured, so poor cleaning never leads to deductions. This is **relative failure**: part of the VfM is lost.

The root causes in every step are process causes: political rush, unrealistic timescales, poor preparation and weak structuring.

examTraps.trap: Thinking that stopping a project during appraisal is always a failure to avoid.
examTraps.fix: The Guide says a decision part-way through not to proceed as a PPP is not negative; it is the purpose of progressive appraisal. The costly failure is cancelling late, especially after tender launch.

examTraps.trap: Confusing absolute contract failure with relative project failure.
examTraps.fix: Absolute failure: the government must rescue or re-tender the contract (serious default or SPV bankruptcy). Relative failure: the contract continues but part of the expected VfM is lost.

examTraps.trap: Believing that signing the contract means the PPP has succeeded.
examTraps.fix: Signature only closes the first stage. The contract can still fail during its life, and success means delivering the expected VfM throughout.

examTraps.trap: Assuming hiring experienced advisers solves the capacity problem.
examTraps.fix: Advisers are highly recommended, but the Guide says they alone are not a solution; the government must build and retain in-house skills.

examTraps.trap: Blaming every failure on the PPP model itself.
examTraps.fix: Some failures come from events that would hurt a traditional project equally. PPP fails as a mechanism when the contract lacks flexibility or when the process is poorly managed.

keyTerms.meaning: Any failure to achieve the Value for Money expected from the project.
A step-by-step process with approvals at each stage, so that weak projects are stopped early and cheaply.
A failure after signature where the government must rescue or re-tender the contract.
A situation where the contract continues but part of the expected VfM is lost.
The specialised skills and resources the government needs to prepare, tender and manage PPPs.
A senior person who leads and advocates the project or program inside government.
A bias that makes people believe they are less at risk of a bad outcome than others, for example an unrealistic traffic forecast.
Problems created by the contract itself, for example a lack of flexibility or unclear risk allocation.
Whether the project will attract quality bidders, investors and lenders.

summary: Project failure means not achieving the expected VfM.
Success needs the right project, the right delivery model, and good appraisal, preparation, structuring and management.
Before signature, a project may be redefined or cancelled; the later the failure, the higher the loss, so use a gateway process.
After signature, failure is absolute (rescue or re-tender) or relative (partial VfM loss).
Weak capacity, political rush, unclear ownership and poor communication are common threats; advisers alone are not enough.
Most contract-life failures trace back to poor appraisal, preparation or structuring.
Bidders want projects that are sound, suitable, feasible, bankable, legal, affordable, well prepared and well structured.

slides.title: What does failure mean?
points: Failure means losing the expected Value for Money
Right project, right model, right management
VfM must be protected for the whole life
slides.narration: Let's start with a clear definition. In the PPP Guide, a project fails when it does not deliver the Value for Money that was expected. That can happen long before construction, or twenty years into the contract. To succeed, three things must be true. It must be the right project, PPP must be the right way to deliver it, and it must be appraised, prepared, structured and managed well. In short, success is good risk management, from the first idea to the final hand-back.

slides.title: Failure before signature
points: Project redefined and re-appraised
Project cancelled, at least as a PPP
Stopping early is not a bad decision
Cancelling after tender launch is worst
slides.narration: Before the contract is signed, a project can fail in two ways. It can be paused and redefined, or it can be cancelled as a PPP. Here is an important exam point. Deciding part-way through not to use a PPP is not a bad thing. That is exactly why we appraise step by step. But the later you stop, the more you lose. That's why the Guide recommends a gateway process with approvals at each stage. The worst case is cancelling after the tender has been launched, because it also damages the government's reputation.

slides.title: Failure after signature
points: Absolute: rescue or re-tender the contract
Caused by serious default or bankruptcy
Relative: part of the VfM is lost
slides.narration: Signing the contract does not mean success. After signature, the Guide describes two grades of failure. Absolute failure is when the government has to rescue the contract or tender it again, usually because the private partner is in serious default or the project company goes bankrupt. Relative failure is quieter. The contract keeps running, but some value leaks away. Perhaps poor performance is not penalised, or the private partner gets an unexpected windfall, or an event occurs that the contract did not foresee.

slides.title: The real causes: process and capacity
points: Poor appraisal, structuring, tender or management
Lack of transaction management capacity
Advisers help but are not enough
Political rush and unrealistic timescales
slides.narration: Some risks, like natural disasters, cannot be avoided, and the contract should be flexible enough to handle them. But many failures start with weak process. The project was not properly appraised, the contract was badly structured, or the tender was badly run. Underneath this, there is often a lack of skills inside government. Good external advisers are highly recommended, but they are not a solution on their own. And in many developing markets, the most common problem is simple: not enough time to prepare, because of political pressure.

slides.title: Governance gaps
points: No standard process or gateway
Unclear institutions and silos
No control of total fiscal exposure
Little transparency or audit
slides.narration: Many failure risks grow when there is no proper PPP framework. Without standard guidelines, each project is prepared differently. Without clear institutions, decisions change and agencies work in silos. Without fiscal rules, a ministry may commit to more PPPs than the country can afford, especially if it thinks someone else will pay. And without disclosure and audit, transparency suffers, the public loses trust, and corruption can grow. The good news is that most of these problems can be reduced by building a proper framework, which is our next lesson.

slides.title: Where failures really start
points: Optimistic CBA or unconfirmed scope
Land, utilities or permits not secured
No bids: short bid period, no market notice
Defaults from aggressive bids or unmanageable risks
slides.narration: The Guide gives many examples, and the exam likes to test them. Look for the phase where the cause really lies. A hospital cancelled because land problems were missed? That's weak appraisal. No bids because the bid period was too short, or fell over a holiday? That's poor tender design. A private partner insolvent because traffic forecasts were too optimistic? Again, weak appraisal. Most failures during the contract were actually planted much earlier, during preparation and structuring.

slides.title: What good bidders want
points: Sound, suitable and feasible project
Bankable and affordable
Properly prepared and structured
Reliable timetable and fair tender
slides.narration: Finally, let's look through the eyes of the bidders. Of course they want a fair return and a bankable project. But they also care about things you might not expect. They want the project to be good for society, because a weak project may lose political support. They want it to be affordable, because an unaffordable project raises the risk that the government will not pay. And they want a reliable timetable and a fair, transparent tender. So, good bidders and a good government actually want the same thing: a well-prepared project.

quiz.question: According to the Guide, which of the following best describes a project failure in a PPP?
options: Any change to the project scope after the Identification Phase
Any project that ends up being delivered by traditional procurement
A failure to achieve the Value for Money expected from the project
Any dispute between the procuring authority and the private partner
quiz.explanation: The Guide defines project failure as a failure to achieve the expected VfM. Deciding during appraisal not to use a PPP is not in itself a failure, and a single dispute does not necessarily mean VfM is lost.

quiz.question: Which situation represents the highest impact failure before contract signature?
options: Cancelling a project after the tender has been launched
Deciding during appraisal that the project should not be a PPP
Partially redefining the project's business terms before launch
Refining the scope after the screening report
quiz.explanation: The Guide says the worst situation before signature is cancellation after tender launch, which wastes time and money and harms the government's PPP reputation. Early decisions to stop or redefine are the purpose of progressive appraisal.

quiz.question: Consider two statements. 1. Reaching contract signature under the conditions of the RFP means the PPP has succeeded. 2. A decision part-way through the process not to proceed with a project as a PPP is not a negative decision.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: Signature does not guarantee success because the contract can still fail during its life, so statement 1 is false. Stopping during progressive appraisal is precisely its purpose, so statement 2 is true.

quiz.question: After contract signature, the government has to re-tender a PPP because the SPV has gone bankrupt. How does the Guide classify this?
options: Relative project failure
Redefinition of the project
Contract risk only
Absolute contract failure
quiz.explanation: Absolute contract failure is when the government must rescue or re-tender the contract, for example because of serious default or bankruptcy. Relative failure means the contract continues with only a partial loss of VfM.

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'The ultimate cause of poor management of the PPP process is often a lack of ____.'
options: private sector equity
transaction management capacity
long-term bank lending
unsolicited proposals
quiz.explanation: The Guide identifies a lack of transaction management capacity, meaning specialised skills and resources, as the frequent root cause. Equity and lending relate to commercial feasibility, not process management.

quiz.question: Which of the following statements about external advisers is consistent with the Guide?
options: Their support is highly recommended, but the government must also develop in-house skills
They remove the need for the government to build its own PPP team
They should only be used after the contract has been signed
They should replace the project champion inside government
quiz.explanation: The Guide says experienced advisers alone are not a solution, although their support is highly recommended for appraisal, preparation, structuring and tender. Building and retaining in-house skills is still essential.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT listed in the Guide as a common project management or governance factor that can compromise a PPP?
options: Political rush and unrealistic timescales
Lack of a champion
Using a gateway process with progressive approvals
Frequent changes in the project team
quiz.explanation: A gateway process is recommended by the Guide as a way to reduce failure. Political rush, lack of a champion and team changes are all listed as threats.

quiz.question: A tender receives no qualifying bids. Which cause is given in the Guide as an example of this type of failure?
options: The winning consortium's bid was too aggressive
A losing bidder challenged the award decision
The government could not afford contingent payments
The bid period was too short or fell over a known holiday period
quiz.explanation: A too-short bid period, or one over a holiday, is listed among the reasons for no bids. Aggressive bids and unaffordable contingent payments cause failures during the contract, and an award challenge happens after award.

quiz.question: Consider two statements about bidders' concerns. 1. Bidders are concerned about affordability because an unaffordable project increases the risk of government breach. 2. Bidders are concerned about a project's economic value because weak value raises the risk of termination or renegotiation.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: The Guide states that private partners care about affordability to avoid government breach, and about economic value because poor value raises the risk of termination or renegotiation. Both statements are true.

quiz.question: Which risk factor is linked in the Guide to the absence of a proper PPP framework?
options: Force majeure events such as floods and earthquakes
A ministry pursuing PPPs beyond what is affordable because it believes it can shift costs elsewhere
Lenders requiring step-in rights in the direct agreement
Bidders forming consortia to combine construction and operation skills
quiz.explanation: The Guide warns that without a proper framework a ministry that thinks it can shift costs may commit to unaffordable PPPs. Force majeure is an unavoidable external risk, and step-in rights and consortia are normal features of PPPs.

quiz.question: According to the Guide, when should the PPP option be adopted for a project?
options: When the public budget has no money for the capital cost in the current year
When there is significant evidence that it adds VfM compared with other methods
When at least three private bidders have already shown interest in the project
When the project is too complex for the ministry to manage on its own
quiz.explanation: The Guide says PPP should only be adopted with significant evidence that it adds incremental VfM compared with other procurement methods (Ch 1 §8). Lack of budget cash is not a valid reason on its own.

quiz.question: Which of the following best describes the Guide's view of success in managing the PPP process?
options: Attracting the highest possible number of bidders to each tender
Transferring as many risks as possible to the private partner
Effective risk management: avoiding or mitigating failure risks
Reaching contract signature within the timetable set in the RFP
quiz.explanation: Success means avoiding project failure risks or mitigating their consequences, which is in essence effective risk management (Ch 1 §8.1). Signature alone does not mean success.

quiz.question: Which is NOT one of the three conditions for success listed in the Guide?
options: The project is appraised, prepared, structured and managed well
PPP is the right delivery model for the chosen project
The project is the right project and is properly prioritised
The private partner earns the highest possible equity return
quiz.explanation: The three conditions are the right project, PPP as the right delivery model, and good appraisal, preparation, structuring and management (Ch 1 §8.1). A maximum private return is not a success condition.

quiz.question: A ministry's own team has prepared an appraisal that strongly favours its preferred project. What does the Guide say may be needed at times?
options: An independent appraiser to ensure objectivity
A second tender to test the appraisal results
A lenders' technical adviser to approve the CBA
A political champion to sign off the appraisal
quiz.explanation: The Guide notes that at times an independent appraiser may be brought in to ensure objectivity (Ch 1 §8.1). A champion leads the project but does not provide an unconflicted review.

quiz.question: Consider two statements. 1. VfM has to be protected only until the contract is signed. 2. Standard approaches and good practices are among the paramount conditions for PPP success.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: VfM must be protected throughout preparation, implementation and the whole life of the contract, so statement 1 is false. Following standard approaches and good practice, with proper process management and resources, is a paramount condition, so statement 2 is true (Ch 1 §8).

quiz.question: A project team finds during appraisal that the scope must be changed, so it goes back and restarts the appraisal. What type of failure is this?
options: Definitive cancellation of the project as a PPP
Full redefinition of the project before signature
Relative project failure after contract signature
Partial redefinition of the business terms only
quiz.explanation: Full redefinition changes the scope and starts the appraisal again; partial redefinition only refines some scope or business terms (Ch 1 §8.1). Both happen before signature, so relative failure does not apply.

quiz.question: Which describes the two categories of failure, in terms of consequences, during preparation and tender?
options: The SPV seriously defaults, or the SPV goes bankrupt
The award is challenged, or the winner refuses to sign
Suspension with redefinition, or definitive cancellation
The contract is rescued, or the contract is re-tendered
quiz.explanation: Before signature the Guide names two categories: suspension with redefinition, and definitive cancellation, at least as a PPP (Ch 1 §8.1). Default and bankruptcy are causes of absolute failure after signature.

quiz.question: Why does the Guide advocate a step-by-step process with progressive approvals (a gateway process)?
options: It removes the need for a separate affordability assessment
It allows the tender to be launched before the appraisal ends
Lenders require a gateway approval before they sign any loans
The more advanced the process, the higher the loss from a failure
quiz.explanation: Losses grow the further the process advances, which is the ultimate reason for progressive approvals (Ch 1 §8.1). A gateway process adds checks; it does not skip appraisal or affordability.

quiz.question: Which is an example of relative project failure given in the Guide?
options: Compensation due for an unforeseen event was never budgeted
The SPV goes bankrupt and the contract has to be re-tendered
The tender receives no qualifying bids from the market
The appraisal shows the project should not be a PPP
quiz.explanation: Relative failure includes unforeseen events not provided for in the contract, or a government not prepared in budget terms to pay compensation due (Ch 1 §8.1). SPV bankruptcy with re-tender is absolute contract failure.

quiz.question: Consider two statements. 1. A change of administration that withdraws political support can reduce the perceived VfM of a project. 2. A government may breach a PPP contract because budget limits were not properly considered in the affordability analysis when the project was approved.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: Political support can change under a new administration and seriously impede perceived VfM (Ch 1 §8.1). The Guide also lists a government that cannot afford payments, because budget limits were not considered in the affordability analysis, as a breach by the grantor (Ch 1 §8.3.2). Both statements are true.

quiz.question: When does PPP fail as a procurement mechanism, in the Guide's view?
options: Whenever the government changes after a national election
Whenever the private partner earns less than it had expected
When the contract lacks flexibility to handle unforeseen events
Whenever a force majeure event affects the construction works
quiz.explanation: Force majeure and unforeseen events cannot be avoided; PPP fails as a mechanism when the contract does not give the parties flexibility to deal with them (Ch 1 §8.2). The event itself is not the failure.

quiz.question: Consider two statements about project failure. 1. Every project failure is a failure of PPP as a procurement mechanism. 2. Some failures would hurt a traditionally procured project equally or even more.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: The Guide says not all project failures are failures of PPP as a mechanism, so statement 1 is false. For some failures the impact would be equal or greater under traditional delivery, so statement 2 is true (Ch 1 §8.2).

quiz.question: Complete the sentence: 'Problems created by the contract itself are sometimes called ____.'
options: counterparty risk
optimism bias
political risk
contract risk
quiz.explanation: The Guide says the contract itself may be a source of risks, sometimes defined as 'contract risk' (Ch 1 §8.2). Optimism bias is an error in forecasts, not a feature of the contract.

quiz.question: Why does the Guide link contract management failures to project preparation?
options: Contract managers are the same people who wrote the appraisal
Lenders approve the contract management plan at appraisal
The management strategy must be built into the contract when drafted
Contract management legally begins before the tender is launched
quiz.explanation: Poor contract management is related to preparation because the contract management strategy must be considered, and provisions included, when the contract is drafted (Ch 1 §8.2).

quiz.question: A PPP unit loses three project directors in two years, and each new director reopens key decisions. Which Box 1.30 factor does this show?
options: Lack of continuity and succession planning in the team
Failure to identify the project stakeholders early
Absence of a fiscal management framework for PPPs
Once-off procurement of an extremely unique project
quiz.explanation: Frequent changes in the project team, with no succession planning, is listed in Box 1.30 (Ch 1 §8.2). The fiscal framework point belongs to the framework risk factors, not to project management.

quiz.question: A ministry's PPP decisions are often reversed by outside officials, and its team has little delegated power. Which Box 1.30 factor is this?
options: Political rush and unrealistic timescales
Lack of proper quality control mechanisms
Failure in taking and managing decisions
Failure to communicate with investors
quiz.explanation: Box 1.30 lists failure in taking and managing decisions, caused by insufficient delegation of powers or external interference (Ch 1 §8.2). Quality control and communication are separate factors.

quiz.question: Which describes a very common source of PPP failure in EMDEs, according to the Guide?
options: Too much long-term finance in the local markets
Too little time for solid preparation and risk analysis
Too much in-house capacity in procuring authorities
Too many bidders competing for each single project
quiz.explanation: Especially in EMDEs, a common source of failure is the lack of time for solid preparation and risk analysis, under political pressure and unrealistic expectations (Ch 1 §8.2).

quiz.question: In countries with little PPP experience, the Guide warns about players who seek advantage through influence or shortcuts. With which route is this particularly common?
options: Two-stage tenders with prequalification
Preferred bidder debt funding competitions
Competitive dialogue
Unsolicited proposals (USPs)
quiz.explanation: The Guide says players who do not follow the rules and seek advantage through influence or shortcuts are particularly common with USPs (Ch 1 §8.2). Competitive processes reduce, not create, this danger.

quiz.question: Which consequence does the Guide link to a complex and unclear institutional framework?
options: Faster approval of unsolicited proposals
Lower construction costs through competition
Contradictory directions and changes in decisions
Higher interest rates on the project debt
quiz.explanation: A complex and unclear institutional framework makes stakeholder management difficult and may create contradictory directions and changes in decisions (Ch 1 §8.2).

quiz.question: A country has no framework to control its total exposure to PPP commitments. What may happen, according to the Guide?
options: Lower bid prices because of much stronger competition
Unexpected conflicts, even termination of an announced process
Automatic approval of all projects by the finance ministry
A legal ban on grants and public loans for all PPP projects
quiz.explanation: Without a fiscal management framework controlling aggregate PPP exposure, unexpected conflicts can arise and a PPP process may be terminated even after it was announced (Ch 1 §8.2).

quiz.question: Consider two statements about a missing PPP framework. 1. A ministry that does not bear project risks may not ensure the private sector bears enough risk. 2. Agencies working in silos may fail to coordinate enough to make PPPs happen.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: Both are listed as risk factors when there is no appropriate PPP framework: a ministry not bearing risks may not be diligent about risk transfer, and silo agencies may fail to coordinate (Ch 1 §8.2).

quiz.question: Which consequence does the Guide link to missing information disclosure provisions?
options: Less transparency and competition, which may feed corruption
Faster tenders because fewer documents need to be published
Better construction quality because bidders compete in secret
A lower WACC because lenders face less public pressure
quiz.explanation: Without disclosure provisions, transparency and competition suffer, harming private interest, public acceptance and political commitment, and this may increase corruption in a vicious circle (Ch 1 §8.2).

quiz.question: An appraisal-phase CBA is much worse than the identification-phase result, because the earlier estimate used over-optimistic assumptions. Where does the real cause lie?
options: In the tender evaluation criteria written in the RFP
In the lenders' due diligence before financial close
In poor contract management during the later operations phase
In poor screening at identification, including optimism bias
quiz.explanation: The Guide gives this as a pre-tender example: the CBA was not done earlier or used overly optimistic assumptions (Ch 1 §8.3.1). Optimism bias is one of the most common reasons for cancelling projects.

quiz.question: Before tender launch, a hospital PPP is abandoned because legal limits on land availability were never checked. What kind of failure is this?
options: An absolute contract failure after signature
A pre-tender failure caused by weak appraisal
A tender failure caused by a competitor challenge
A relative failure caused by weak performance
quiz.explanation: Land limits for a hospital not detected in appraisal is the Guide's example of a project abandoned before tender launch (Ch 1 §8.3.1). No contract exists yet, so absolute or relative failure cannot apply.

quiz.question: A tender is suspended after launch because the public and civil society strongly oppose the project. Which preparation weakness does the Guide link to this?
options: The contract lacked measurable performance standards
The bid period fell over a well-known national holiday
The SPV's minimum equity requirement was set too low
Project information was not made public in time for comments
quiz.explanation: The Guide lists strong stakeholder opposition and failure to publish project information in time for suggestions as reasons for suspending a tender (Ch 1 §8.3.1). A holiday bid period explains no bids, not opposition.

quiz.question: Which would NOT explain an empty tender with zero compliant offers, according to the Guide?
options: The government was seen as not honouring similar PPP contracts
The authority told the market about the project well in advance
The tender was launched without any advance notice to the market
The contract as designed was not financially or technically feasible
quiz.explanation: Missing advance notice, an unfeasible contract, and a perception that government does not honour other PPP contracts are all listed causes of no bids (Ch 1 §8.3.1). Early notice to the market helps, rather than harms, competition.

quiz.question: A contract is awarded, but the successful bidder refuses to sign it. Which cause does the Guide give for this?
options: The project had not been properly prepared
The bid bond required in the RFP was too low
The bid period had been longer than usual
The authority had shortlisted the bidders first
quiz.explanation: The Guide says a contract may be awarded but not signed because a competitor challenges the award, or because the winner refuses to sign due to a lack of project preparation (Ch 1 §8.3.1). A long bid period or a shortlist is not given as a cause.

quiz.question: Environmental permits are at risk because the authority managed the process badly, and financing does not close. How does the Guide categorise this?
options: A pre-signature failure from unresolved preparation problems
A minor failure caused by an unclear risk allocation
A default by the private partner through lack of capacity
A relative failure during the life of the contract
quiz.explanation: Financing not closing because of unresolved preparation problems, such as permits at risk from poor authority management, is a failure before the contract takes effect (Ch 1 §8.3.1). The cause lies with the authority, not the private partner.

quiz.question: Construction is badly delayed because the government never secured access to the land. What does the Guide say lies behind this?
options: Overly aggressive pricing in the private partner's bid
Weak step-in rights in the lenders' direct agreement
Weak government due diligence on risks it retained
A force majeure event outside anyone's control
quiz.explanation: The Guide gives construction delay from missing land or right of way as a result of the government's lack of due diligence on the risks it assumes (Ch 1 §8.3.2). It is a preparation failure, not force majeure.

quiz.question: The winning consortium's bid was so aggressive that it later defaults. According to the Guide, what should the tender have done?
options: Been structured to detect or avoid overly aggressive offers
Allowed the bidder to renegotiate the price after signing
Awarded the contract to the lowest price without any checks
Required the government to guarantee the SPV's equity return
quiz.explanation: The Guide says default from an overly aggressive bid shows the tender was not structured to avoid or detect overly optimistic offers (Ch 1 §8.3.2). Guaranteeing returns or renegotiating would destroy VfM.

quiz.question: A private partner cannot meet its minimum service standards because the authority set requirements no operator could achieve. What does the Guide identify as the cause of this default?
options: A lack of capacity assessment during the tender
An over-optimistic traffic forecast in the appraisal
Interface works that the government did not deliver
Unrealistic performance requirements set by government
quiz.explanation: One listed cause of private partner default is the government setting unrealistic performance requirements (Ch 1 §8.3.2). Capacity not being assessed is a different cause, about the consortium itself.

quiz.question: An SPV becomes insolvent because the traffic forecast used in the appraisal was far too optimistic. What is the root cause?
options: Weak lender step-in rights
Poor appraisal of the project
Excessive public co-financing
Poor hand-back of the assets
quiz.explanation: The Guide's example of contractor insolvency is a project found unfeasible because of poor appraisal, such as a too-optimistic traffic forecast (Ch 1 §8.3.2). The failure shows during the contract but was caused earlier.

quiz.question: A government is responsible for the civil works on a rail PPP but fails to deliver them on time, so the private partner cannot run its systems. How does the Guide classify this?
options: Relative failure through weak performance measures
Force majeure affecting both parties equally
Absolute failure through private partner default
A government breach through failed interfacing works
quiz.explanation: The Guide lists the government failing to perform interfacing works, such as civil works for a rail project, as a breach by the grantor (Ch 1 §8.3.2). The private partner is not in default here.

quiz.question: Which is an example of a minor failure or loss of VfM given in the Guide?
options: Cancellation of the tender after it has been launched
Costly disputes arising from an unclear risk allocation
No qualifying bids received from the market at all
Bankruptcy of the SPV during the construction period
quiz.explanation: Minor failures include costly disputes from unclear risk allocation and performance requirements that cannot be measured or enforced (Ch 1 §8.3.2). Cancellation after launch is the worst pre-signature failure.

quiz.question: Consider two statements about the private sector's view. 1. Bidders expect the process to follow the announced timetable. 2. Commercial feasibility is a necessary condition for a PPP, and it requires bankability.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: The Guide says bidders want a reliable timetable and collaborative process management, and that commercial feasibility, which needs bankability, is a necessary condition (Ch 1 §8.4). Both statements are true.

quiz.question: According to Table 1.7, why do bidders want a project to be economically sound?
options: Low use weakens public commitment and can hurt demand revenue
It allows the SPV to avoid all performance deductions
It removes the need for the lenders' due diligence
It guarantees that grants will be paid during construction
quiz.explanation: A project that fails as a solution, for example with use far below expectations, risks weaker public commitment and can compromise financial feasibility in demand projects (Ch 1 §8.4, Table 1.7).

quiz.question: According to Table 1.7, what is likely if a project that is unsuitable for PPP is tendered as a PPP?
options: An artificial risk structure brings no bids or later failure
The government must convert it into a grant-funded project
Lenders must accept a lower margin to support the project
It automatically becomes an institutional PPP with public control
quiz.explanation: Table 1.7 says an unsuitable project tendered as a PPP will have an artificial, inefficient risk structure, likely leading to no bids or failures later (Ch 1 §8.4).

quiz.question: In Table 1.7, which condition means the payment ceiling covers all costs, risk contingencies and a fair return?
options: Legally feasible
Economically sound
Properly prepared
Commercially feasible
quiz.explanation: Commercial feasibility means the payment limit or price covers all costs and risk contingencies, plus a return in line with the cost of capital (Ch 1 §8.4, Table 1.7). Economic soundness is about being the right solution.

quiz.question: Why do good bidders want a properly structured tender with balanced but high capacity requirements?
options: To remove the need for technical proposals in the bid
To reduce the number of lenders able to join the project
To allow the winner to sell its shares during construction
To avoid unfair competition from unrealistic, aggressive offers
quiz.explanation: Table 1.7 says reputable players want high capacity requirements and technical proposals to avoid unfair competition from unrealistic and aggressive offers (Ch 1 §8.4).

quiz.question: Under Table 1.7, what does 'properly prepared' require for the risks transferred to the private sector?
options: Consistent and available information, such as utilities data
A price adjustment each year for any cost increase
An equity stake by the authority in the SPV
A guarantee that government insures all of those risks
quiz.explanation: A properly prepared project has enough due diligence, and for transferred risks the information must be consistent and available, for example environmental approvals and utilities allocation (Ch 1 §8.4, Table 1.7).
